newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi court adjourns British nurses murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Saudi court adjourns British nurses murder trial.

text.p: A Saudi court trying two British nurses for the murder of an Australian colleague adjourned on Sunday to give the victim's lawyers time to produce vital documents, legal sources said.
"The court adjourned till June 23...The judges, requested evidence that the victim's brother was her legal heir," sources close to the defence attorneys said.

Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, are charged with killing 55-year-old Australian colleague Yvonne Gilford at the King Fahd medical complex in nearby Dhahran last December. Medical reports said Gilford had been stabbed 13 times, bludgeoned and suffocated.
If convicted, they could face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally carried out by public beheading.
The sources said the defence lawyers questioned the legal right of Frank Gilford, the victim's brother, to demand the imposition of death penalty.

Islamic sharia law enforced in Saudi Arabia allows the victim's family to decide for or against execution if the court determines capital punishment is the appropriate sentence. Gilford's brother Frank has said he favours the death penalty.
Alternatively, the victim's family could ask for financial recompense, commonly known as "blood money".

Sources close to the court said the two nurses who have been detained at the central prison in nearby Dammam, attended the hearing. They arrived with shackled feet and wearing the long black robes women must wear in the conservative kingdom.
The trial had been adjourned on May 25 to allow Gilford's family time to consider a pre-verdict settlement which could spare the defendants' lives.
A statement issued by the Saudi Embassy in London over the weekend said that even if the court found the two women guilty of killing Gilford, they would not necessarily be put to death.
For example, the court could find the murder involved self-defence or resulted from an argument which got out of hand, in which case the death penalty would not be applied, it said.

A verdict was only the first stage of the trial, the embassy said. If the death penalty was imposed the case would go automatically to a five-judge appeal court. It would then proceed through several other legal bodies and the sentence would have to be approved by King Fahd before it was carried out.
